description: Recon Village at DEF CON 25 covers reconnaissance and OSINT techniques for information gathering, asset discovery, and attack surface mapping. The 15 talks explore social media analysis, domain discovery, source code research, and practical OSINT methodologies.

talks.title: DFIR Automation Orchestration Tools For OSINT Recon
talks.teaser: Automate OSINT reconnaissance and digital forensics through orchestration tools that streamline attack surface discovery.
talks.summary:
### Bridging the Gap Between DFIR and OSINT
At 00:00, Tyler Rorabaugh takes the stage at the Recon Village to present a practical methodology for modern investigators: applying Digital Forensics and Incident Response (DFIR) automation and orchestration concepts directly to Open Source Intelligence (OSINT). Rorabaugh explains that while corporate security teams have successfully automated incident response playbooks to handle malware alerts, intelligence analysts still conduct OSINT reconnaissance through tedious, manual web searches that hinder investigative scalability.

### The Power of Security Orchestration and Automation (SOAR)
At 04:15 and 09:07, Rorabaugh reviews the emergence of Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response (SOAR) platforms, highlighting tools like Rapid7 Komand, Demisto, and open-source workflow frameworks. He explains how SOAR architectures utilize modular plugins and standardized API connectors to automate sequential workflows—ingesting input indicators, triggering external data lookups, evaluating logical conditions, and formatting structured outputs without human intervention.

### Constructing Automated Reconnaissance Playbooks
At 12:40, the speaker demonstrates constructing an end-to-end automated OSINT pipeline. In his demonstration playbook, an investigator supplies a single target domain name. The orchestration engine automatically executes multiple tasks concurrently: querying DNS servers for subdomains, running WHOIS lookups to identify registrant email addresses, querying certificate transparency logs, checking domain reputation across threat feeds, and executing reverse IP lookups to identify shared hosting infrastructure.

### Integrating Threat Feeds and Social Media Enumeration
At 15:30, Rorabaugh details integrating specialized intelligence sources into orchestration playbooks. He demonstrates pulling passive DNS historical data, querying Shodan for exposed ports and industrial control banners, and automating username searches across social media platforms. By standardizing investigative playbooks, intelligence teams can ensure that every target is subjected to a consistent, comprehensive baseline investigation within seconds.

### Scalable Intelligence Operations and Analyst Empowerment
Concluding between 17:15 and 18:19, Rorabaugh emphasizes that automation does not replace human analytical intuition: rather, it eliminates repetitive data gathering. By automating the mechanical aspects of information gathering, intelligence analysts can dedicate their cognitive energy to complex correlation, behavioral profiling, and strategic decision-making. He encourages researchers to publish open-source automation modules to advance collective OSINT capabilities.

talks.title: Winner Announcement Prize Distribution
talks.teaser: Recognition and prize distribution for contest winners and top performers in the Recon Village.
talks.summary:
### Concluding the DEF CON 25 Recon Village CTF
At 00:03, the organizers of the Recon Village open the closing ceremonies and prize distribution for the inaugural Recon Village Open Source Intelligence (OSINT) Capture The Flag (CTF) competition. The organizers express immense gratitude to the hundreds of participants who competed, noting that the remarkable turnout and competitive energy exceeded all expectations for the village's first official CTF event.

### Celebrating Top Teams and Scoreboard Standings
At 03:40 and 07:50, the organizers display the final competition scoreboard and announce the top-performing teams. They celebrate the podium finishers—including teams "Proprietary Data," "Nosey Parkers," "STFU Darling," and "4815162342"—commending their technical tenacity, analytical precision, and collaborative problem-solving across intense rounds of open-source reconnaissance challenges.

### Reviewing Challenging OSINT Puzzles and Methodology
At 11:15, the presentation recaps the diverse challenge categories designed for the CTF. The organizers review complex scenarios that tested competitors' intelligence-gathering capabilities: geolocating obscure physical landmarks from cropped photographs, tracking hidden operational personas across social media networks, inspecting EXIF metadata and hidden document properties, and identifying concealed indicators across public corporate filings.

### Sponsor Recognition and Prize Distribution
At 14:00 and 15:34, the organizers distribute prizes to the winning teams, presenting hardware gear from Hak5, software-defined radio equipment, specialized commercial training vouchers, and commemorative Recon Village challenge coins. They extend sincere appreciation to the industry sponsors and volunteer infrastructure engineers whose generous support made the competition possible.

### Looking Ahead to Future Recon Village Initiatives
Concluding the ceremony, the village coordinators thank the broader DEF CON community for welcoming the Recon Village into the conference family. They invite participants to provide constructive feedback on challenge design, encourage competitors to author public write-ups of their investigative methodologies, and pledge to expand CTF infrastructure and educational workshops for upcoming DEF CON events.

talks.title: OSINT Tactics on Source Code and Developers
talks.teaser: OSINT techniques for tracking developers, analyzing public source code, and identifying sensitive information exposed in repositories.
talks.summary:
### Reconnaissance via Source Code and Developer Footprints
At 00:00, Simon Roses introduces open-source intelligence (OSINT) methodologies focused on public source code repositories and developer profiles. While traditional reconnaissance emphasizes network perimeter scanning, domain registration, and DNS enumeration, modern software development workflows leave vast trails of sensitive metadata in public codebases that adversaries can exploit.

### Mining Commit Histories, Metadata, and Organizational Charts
At 06:06 and 11:00, Roses explains how analyzing Git repositories and commit logs allows an investigator to map an organization's internal structure. Examining author email addresses, commit timestamps, and collaborator networks reveals working hours, developer roles, and team handoffs, providing critical context for targeted social engineering and phishing campaigns.

### Uncovering Secrets, Hardcoded Credentials, and Obsolete Code
At 18:00 and 24:01, the speaker demonstrates extracting actionable intelligence from source code comments, TODO notes, and embedded configuration files. Developers frequently leave behind hardcoded API keys, internal database connection strings, test credentials, and architecture diagrams that bypass external network perimeters.

### Automated Repository Parsing and Relational Threat Modeling
At 30:00 and 37:01, Roses details building automated ingestion pipelines using custom scripts and PostgreSQL databases to index massive source code repositories. By correlating commit history with compiler warnings, dependency manifests, and external tools like the Tinkerer framework, security analysts can track changes over time and identify newly introduced vulnerabilities before formal deployment.

talks.title: Keynote:  Seeing is Believing   The Future of Recon
talks.teaser: Keynote vision for the evolving landscape of reconnaissance—emerging tools, techniques, and methodologies shaping the future of OSINT.
talks.summary:
### Keynote: The Evolving Landscape of Open Source Intelligence
At 00:00, Shane MacDougall takes the stage to deliver the keynote address for the Recon Village, titled "Seeing is Believing: The Future of Recon." MacDougall surveys the profound evolution of Open Source Intelligence (OSINT) over the preceding decade, tracing its transition from an informal, ad-hoc discipline practiced by hobbyists into an essential, highly scrutinized component of corporate threat intelligence, national security, and investigative journalism.

### The Threat of Data Poisoning and Weaponized Misinformation
At 08:30 and 15:15, MacDougall delivers a warning regarding the vulnerability of public data sources. He explains that as OSINT tools become widely automated, adversaries have begun actively weaponizing data poisoning attacks: seeding public repositories, social media networks, and open-source lists with deliberately falsified indicators, honeypot profiles, and disinformation. Investigators who blindly trust automated tool scrapers risk being manipulated by sophisticated counter-reconnaissance campaigns.

### High-Resolution Geospatial Analysis and Environmental Clues
At 22:42, the speaker demonstrates advanced geolocation techniques using high-resolution commercial satellite imagery, street-level photography, and environmental analysis. He illustrates how expert investigators can pinpoint exact geographic coordinates anywhere on earth by correlating sun angles, shadow lengths, vehicle models, overhead power line configurations, and architectural building styles, proving that visual imagery contains vast layers of forensic evidence beyond immediate pixel content.

### Regulatory Pressures, GDPR, and the Shrinking Open Web
At 31:10 and 37:25, MacDougall analyzes the regulatory headwinds confronting open reconnaissance. The impending enforcement of global privacy legislation, most notably the European Union's GDPR, threatens to redact WHOIS domain registries and restrict public access to corporate ownership records. He explores how the progressive walling-off of social media APIs forces intelligence practitioners to develop resilient, ethical collection methodologies that do not rely on fragile third-party platforms.

### The Ethical Boundaries of Reconnaissance
Concluding between 41:30 and 43:49, MacDougall delivers an impassioned plea regarding the ethics of intelligence gathering. He reminds practitioners that the tools used to uncover malicious cyber actors can easily be repurposed for doxxing, harassment, and corporate espionage. He challenges the audience to uphold strict ethical standards, questioning whether their investigations serve legitimate defensive interests or merely cross into privacy invasion for commercial gain.

talks.title: Up Close and Personal: Keeping an Eye On Mobile
talks.teaser: Mobile-focused OSINT techniques for tracking individuals and organizations through mobile devices and location data.
talks.summary:
### Mobile Application Reconnaissance for Security Assessments
At 00:00, Mikhail Sosonkin, Director of Research and Data at Synack, introduces methodologies for conducting deep reconnaissance against modern mobile applications on iOS and Android. Sosonkin highlights how mobile apps frequently expose sensitive backend attack surfaces that traditional web assessments overlook.

### Overcoming ARM Architecture and Static Analysis Barriers
At 02:31, Sosonkin discusses the learning curve associated with reversing compiled ARM binaries. He explains how binary obfuscation, encrypted strings, and proprietary packers complicate static analysis, inspiring him to develop helper tools such as IDARef to speed up assembly instruction comprehension during reverse engineering.

### Dynamic Instrumentation and Code Coverage Tracing
At 05:02, the presentation focuses on dynamic runtime analysis using frameworks like Frida and Cycript. By hooking into runtime method dispatchers, Sosonkin logs executed functions in real-time, mapping out code coverage to verify that automated and manual testing reaches all critical application components.

### In-Memory UI Trees and Infrastructure Endpoint Discovery
At 07:28 and 09:53, Sosonkin demonstrates how inspecting in-memory view hierarchies and object states reveals hidden functionality. By manipulating UI properties and intentionally triggering error routines, testers can induce client applications into leaking undocumented API gateways, staging environments, and backend cloud microservices.

### Workflow Integration and Reconnaissance Tooling
Concluding between 12:11 and 15:20, Sosonkin shares techniques for structuring mobile reconnaissance data. He emphasizes compiling discovered endpoints, auth parameters, and structural graphs into centralized research notebooks to empower comprehensive vulnerability chaining during subsequent testing phases.

talks.title: FERPA: Only Grades Are Safe; OSINT In Higher Education
talks.teaser: Explore OSINT vulnerabilities in higher education systems and how institutions' public data can be exploited to profile students and staff.
talks.summary:
### Higher Education: The Open-Access Security Dilemma
At 00:00, data analyst and researcher Leah Figueroa opens her presentation at the Recon Village by examining the unique cybersecurity posture of higher education. Unlike corporate enterprises that enforce strict network perimeters and data access controls, universities are philosophically designed to be open, collaborative, and publicly accessible environments. Figueroa argues that this open-access culture creates massive reconnaissance opportunities that leave students, faculty, and research data dangerously exposed.

### The Illusory Protection of FERPA
At 05:40 and 11:20, Figueroa deconstructs the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA), the primary federal statute governing student privacy in the United States. She exposes a critical truth: contrary to popular belief, FERPA legally protects only formal academic records—specifically grades, GPA, and transcripts. Non-academic student information is classified as "directory information," which universities can legally publish online unless students actively submit complex opt-out paperwork.

### Harvesting Personal Telemetry from Public University Directories
At 18:20, the speaker demonstrates how easily an adversary can harvest granular student profiles using OSINT techniques. Through public campus directories, student athlete rosters, departmental newsletters, and social media groups, researchers can scrape student home addresses, personal phone numbers, campus employment schedules, dorm locations, and class schedules. Figueroa highlights alarming scenarios where campus health clinics and academic scheduling systems inadvertently leak sensitive personal appointment details.

### Physical Security and Real-World Stalking Risks
At 25:30 and 31:15, the presentation explores the physical safety risks stemming from academic OSINT. Figueroa illustrates how stalkers, abusive ex-partners, or malicious actors can correlate public course schedules with social media check-ins to track students' physical movements across campus in real time. Furthermore, international students and vulnerable populations face heightened risks of state-sponsored harassment and targeted financial fraud enabled by exposed campus directories.

### Reforming Academic Data Policies and Protecting Students
Concluding between 34:10 and 36:39, Figueroa calls for immediate, sweeping reforms in higher education data governance. She urges university administrators to implement privacy-by-default policies, making directory information private unless students explicitly opt in. She advocates for comprehensive privacy awareness training during student orientation, mandatory data minimization across university departments, and regular attack-surface audits to safeguard campus communities.

talks.title: Do Tinder Bots Dream of Electric Toys
talks.teaser: OSINT techniques using dating apps like Tinder for intelligence gathering, profiling, and reconnaissance operations.
talks.summary:
### Deconstructing Dating App Bots and Algorithmic Profiles
At 00:00, Inbar Raz (former Principal Researcher at PerimeterX) opens an investigative presentation examining the proliferation of automated bots on the popular dating application Tinder. Raz outlines how commercial bot operators exploit Tinder's mobile API and image-heavy interface to engage with millions of users at scale.

### Anatomy of Fake Profiles and Social Engineering
At 02:01 and 05:00, Raz documents his field research tracking fake profiles across international conferences, from Copenhagen to Las Vegas. He demonstrates how bot operators systematically scrape high-resolution glamour photos, social media models, and adult entertainer images to construct persuasive profiles designed to maximize right-swipes and initiate conversations.

### Dissecting Automated Chat Scripts and Off-Platform Redirections
At 08:00 and 15:00, the presentation details the conversational mechanics employed by Tinder bots. Using pre-scripted conversational trees, bots initiate flirtatious dialogue before delivering shortened URLs or messaging app handles. Raz analyzes the redirect chains behind these links, showing how users are funneled through affiliate networks, fraudulent webcam services, and recurring subscription billing traps.

### Infrastructure Attribution: Affiliate Networks and Exploits
At 18:00 and 25:00, Raz investigates the backend infrastructure supporting bot campaigns. By capturing network traffic and dissecting HTTP request headers, he traces affiliate referral codes, advertising networks, and hosting servers. He emphasizes the serious security risks posed by unvetted off-platform links, including mobile exploit kits, credential harvesting pages, and drive-by malware infections.

### Corporate Platform Responsibility and Defense
Concluding at 28:02, Raz addresses the broader legal and security ramifications for dating platforms. He warns that failing to curb malicious bot ecosystems exposes users to financial fraud and mobile compromise while placing platform operators at severe risk of brand degradation and legal liability.

talks.title: How To Obtain 100 Facebooks a Day
talks.teaser: Large-scale Facebook OSINT techniques for bulk intelligence gathering, account enumeration, and relationship mapping.
talks.summary:
### Exploiting Search Indexing to Harvest Facebook Accounts
At 00:00, security researchers Guillermo Buendia and Yael Esquivel demonstrate how search engine discovery techniques can uncover active Facebook account credentials and validation links without direct credential cracking. They explain how automated indexing crawlers ingest sensitive session parameters unintentionally published across the web.

### Mechanism of Shared Validation Links and Session Keys
At 03:42, the speakers analyze Facebook's account validation and quick-login architecture. When users generate temporary recovery links, URL strings embed session tokens and passcode parameters (`p_key`). If these links are posted onto public web forums, paste sites, or URL shorteners, any third party clicking the link instantly authenticates into the victim's profile.

### Advanced Search Dorking and Pattern Matching
At 06:30 and 10:13, Buendia and Esquivel demonstrate search queries (Google dorks) specifically targeting indexed validation endpoints such as `fb.me` and `auth.php`. By combining URL parameter filters with targeted keyword patterns, they demonstrate automated scripts capturing dozens of valid, authenticated profile links daily.

### Security Implications and Developer Mitigations
Concluding between 15:34 and 17:00, the presenters review critical security controls for web identity providers. They recommend binding temporary authentication tokens to user IP addresses and browser fingerprints, enforcing single-use policies with short time-to-live (TTL) expirations, and ensuring authentication endpoints strictly emit `noindex` headers and `robots.txt` disallow directives.

talks.title: An Introduction to Graph Theory for OSINT
talks.teaser: Apply graph theory and network analysis to OSINT data for uncovering relationships, detecting patterns, and mapping organizational structures.
talks.summary:
### Demystifying Graph Theory for Security Analysts
At 00:00, security executive Andrew Hay introduces graph theory concepts tailored for cybersecurity and OSINT practitioners without requiring advanced mathematical training. Drawing from his experience leading data science and research teams at OpenDNS, Hay emphasizes that graph theory provides an intuitive, high-leverage framework for making sense of complex threat data.

### Nodes, Vertices, and Relational Edges
At 02:00 and 06:00, Hay breaks down fundamental graph components: vertices (nodes) representing discrete entities—such as domain names, IP addresses, email handles, or cryptographic hashes—and edges representing the relationships connecting them (e.g., DNS resolution, WHOIS registration, or network traffic). He contrasts directed and undirected graphs, showing how edge orientation reflects data flow and communication hierarchy.

### Graph Centrality and Choke Point Identification
At 09:00 and 15:00, the presentation explores graph centrality metrics that help investigators prioritize intelligence assets. Hay explains degree centrality (measuring total direct connections), betweenness centrality (identifying bridge nodes that control data flow between distinct clusters), and closeness centrality, illustrating how these metrics pinpoint threat actor infrastructure hubs and single points of failure.

### Open-Source Graph Tooling and Workflow Integration
At 18:00 and 24:00, Hay reviews accessible graph analysis tools, highlighting Gephi, Graphviz, Maltego transforms, Neo4j, and Python NetworkX. He demonstrates how analysts can convert flat CSV datasets, network flow logs, and OSINT dumps into interactive graph databases to reveal non-obvious clusters and shared infrastructure.

### Intelligence Hygiene and Avoiding Graph Poisoning
Concluding between 33:01 and 34:01, Hay delivers a crucial warning regarding threat intelligence hygiene. Because graph algorithms amplify connections, analysts must critically evaluate crowd-sourced feeds and automated transforms. Feeding unverified honeypot alerts or contaminated public lists into graph models can generate misleading clusters, reinforcing the necessity of human verification during OSINT investigations.

talks.title: Recon and Bug Bounties What A Great Love Story
talks.teaser: Combining robust reconnaissance techniques with bug bounty hunting to maximize finding and reporting vulnerabilities at scale.
talks.summary:
### Reconnaissance as the Key Differentiator in Bug Bounties
At 00:00, Abhijeth Dugginapeddi shares practical reconnaissance methodologies designed to maximize high-severity findings in competitive bug bounty programs. Dugginapeddi emphasizes that while most hunters attack the primary web properties, comprehensive asset discovery uncovers vulnerable peripheral systems that remain completely untested.

### Target Selection: Fortified Core vs. Forgotten Perimeter
At 05:07, Dugginapeddi contrasts the security posture of an organization's flagship website with its extended digital footprint. Major public-facing assets receive constant scrutiny and rigorous internal testing, whereas forgotten regional portals, staging servers, and third-party SaaS integrations frequently harbor severe misconfigurations and legacy vulnerabilities.

### Automating Subdomain Enumeration and Port Discovery
At 09:44, the speaker covers practical workflows for asset discovery, combining DNS brute-forcing, Certificate Transparency logs, and port scanning to map target infrastructure. He shares real-world case studies where discovering obscure subdomains led directly to exposed internal administrative interfaces and debug consoles.

### JavaScript Scraping and Hidden Endpoint Extraction
At 19:14 and 24:05, Dugginapeddi details the value of parsing client-side JavaScript files using tools like LinkFinder. Minified bundles often contain hardcoded API keys, unauthenticated REST routes, development endpoints, and internal microservice addresses that provide immediate footholds for remote exploitation.

### Rapid Triage and Continuous Asset Monitoring
Concluding between 28:00 and 29:12, Dugginapeddi stresses the importance of setting up automated recon pipelines to monitor targets for newly published assets. He highlights how rapid notification of infrastructure changes enables researchers to report critical vulnerabilities within hours of deployment.
